newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Violence, desolation loom over south Albania polls.
newsitem.headline: Violence, desolation loom over south Albania polls.

text.p: Armed gangs roaming the countryside and a lack of modern communications could turn Sunday's general election into a nightmare for Western observers in southern Albania.

"Communication with remote villages may well be the biggest technical problem we face," said Michael Klinger from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), charged with monitoring the vote.

In this nearly-abandoned village dominated by the ethnic Greek minority near the southern Adriatic port of Sarande, monitors appeared only once to question local officials about security, Aliko village head Vasil Joanu told Reuters.
"We told them that self-defence groups would guard the voting process at all Greek villages but we could not offer guarantees for any others," Joanu said.
Guards have been posted at the entrance to Aliko, near a monument to Albania's wartime resistance against Nazi Germany -- a crumbling concrete pillar jutting from an earth mound.

Defence groups were formed in March after an uprising prompted by the crash of five pyramid savings schemes. Looting of army arsenals put weapons into the hands of youths who have been terrorising the south.
Most of southern Albania's large Greek minority, which is running candidates under the banner of the Party of Human Rights, has fled to Greece to seek work or simply avoid the violence.
Elderly Aliko residents live in fear of the gunmen and say they expect few of their sons and daughters to return to vote.
"How can they come back? There is only death here," said Fotulla Cavo, 67.
Dressed from head-to-toe in black and sporting a Soviet Army belt around her lean waist, Cavo is among 200 people remaining in what was once a village of 1,700.
It takes 40 minutes to drive the three km (two miles) to Aliko on a deeply rutted road from Sarande, past empty farms, forgotten factories and raided army camps.
Horse-drawn carts and donkeys are the only traffic seen on a dirt road strewn with rusting farm machinery.
About 450 OSCE observers are expected to travel through Albania to monitor Sunday's poll, escorted by soldiers from a 7,000-strong, Italian-led multi-national force.
Their task in the cities and major towns of the rebellious south is not expected to be much easier.
In Sarande, where no force is stationed, monitors must tour 22 polling stations and return by nightfall to base in Gjirokaster, 40 km (25 miles) to the north, Klinger said.
That makes it virtually impossible for the observers to monitor the vote count after polls are closed.
Officials in Sarande, population 25,000, say about 11,000 voters have registered to elect three deputies in the 155-seat parliament.
